messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raymond is a 68-year-old married school counselor who has spent the better part of four decades helping adolescents navigate crisis. He presents now as someone in crisis himself, arriving at the intake appointment with the careful composure of a man who has spent years teaching others to name their feelings while remaining, in his own estimation, entirely unable to do so. His PCL-5 score of 62 places him in the severe range, and the clinical picture that emerges across the first few sessions is one of a man whose professional instincts toward connection have been systematically dismantled by what happened to him fourteen months ago.

The assault occurred late on a Friday evening in the parking lot of a bar Raymond had visited with a former colleague. He had not been drinking heavily — a detail he returns to with some bitterness — but the man who attacked him had been. Raymond remembers the smell before anything else: a sharp, sour wave of alcohol on the man's breath as he was shoved against a car door, then struck repeatedly. At some point he lost consciousness. He came around in an emergency room, the antiseptic sting of the air hitting him before he could open his eyes, a nurse leaning close and speaking in the careful, lowered voice people use when they are trying not to frighten you. He was badly concussed, had two broken ribs, and remained in hospital overnight. His wife held his hand. He does not remember much of that part.

What Raymond does remember, he remembers in pieces. He has described the assault not as a continuous narrative but as a sequence of still photographs: the yellow light of the parking lot, the man's face at close range, the specific angle of a fist. Each image arrives complete and discrete, and between them there is nothing — just the sensation of one frame cutting to the next. When a fragment surfaces without warning, as they frequently do, it carries with it the full physiological terror of the original moment: his heart rate spikes, his chest tightens, and for several seconds he is entirely certain he is about to be killed. The memory does not feel like recollection. It feels like recurrence.

The triggers that reliably summon these intrusions have shaped Raymond's daily life in ways that have become increasingly difficult to conceal. The smell of alcohol — encountered at faculty gatherings, at the occasional dinner where wine is poured nearby — sends a fragment crashing forward without warning, and Raymond has responded by withdrawing from most social occasions. He stopped attending the monthly staff dinners at his school, offering scheduling conflicts as explanation. More consequentially, the antiseptic smell of the school nurse's office, which sits two doors from his own, has become nearly intolerable; he now routes himself through a longer corridor to avoid passing it, and a colleague has noticed and asked, with genuine concern, whether he is all right. What troubles Raymond most acutely, however, is the trigger he finds hardest to explain: emotional closeness itself. When a student leans in to confide something painful, or when his wife reaches for him in the particular way she has when she senses he is struggling, something in him recoils. The proximity — the lowered voice, the attentive face — maps onto something in the assault he has not yet been able to articulate, and the memory surfaces.

In response, Raymond has developed a set of strategies that he recognises, with the rueful clarity of a trained counselor, as counterproductive. He avoids people where he can manage it, keeping sessions with students brief and professionally bounded. He has pulled back from his wife in ways that have produced a new and painful distance between them. And when avoidance is not possible — when someone gets emotionally close in a moment he cannot exit — he has learned to dissociate deliberately, to blank out behind attentive eyes, to be present in body while retreating entirely inward. The trouble is that this deliberate withdrawal keeps him in a state of vigilant watchfulness for the very cues he is trying to escape, so that the triggers remain perpetually salient, perpetually capable of pulling the next fragment forward.

What finally brought Raymond to seek help was a session three weeks ago in which a student described being attacked, and Raymond sat across from him, blank and unreachable, aware that he was failing the boy entirely. He came to his first appointment hoping, above all, to be able to do his job again. What he fears most is that the person who was good at it is gone.
